config.title: Build end to end capstone ecommerce frontend in vanilla JS

intro.title: Build end to end capstone ecommerce frontend in vanilla JS
intro.body: In this capstone project, you will build a complete e-commerce storefront from scratch using only vanilla JavaScript. You will create a product catalog, a functional shopping cart, and a checkout flow, learning how to manage state and handle user interactions without any external frameworks. The core programming concepts you will practice include DOM manipulation, event handling, and managing application state with objects and arrays. By the end, you will have a fully interactive, multi-page web application that demonstrates end-to-end frontend development fundamentals.
intro.usecase: This capstone project mirrors the core frontend architecture of real-world ecommerce platforms like Shopify storefronts or Amazon's product browsing experience. You'll implement essential UI patterns such as product grids with dynamic filtering, a persistent shopping cart panel, and a multi-step checkout form—all common in production web applications. Mastering this vanilla JS approach provides a foundational understanding of state management, DOM manipulation, and event handling that directly applies to building custom storefronts, admin dashboards, or any data-driven consumer interface without relying on frameworks.

objectives: Construct a product catalog display that fetches and renders items from a mock API
Implement a shopping cart system that tracks selected items and calculates totals
Configure user interface components for product filtering and search functionality
Integrate form validation and submission for a simulated checkout process
Manipulate the DOM to update cart contents and product availability in real-time
Initialize and manage application state for user sessions and cart persistence
Apply event handling to enable user interactions like adding items and adjusting quantities

steps.title: Import all required modules and libraries
steps.instruction: Import axios from 'axios' for making API calls in your ecommerce frontend.
steps.hint: Use the ES6 import syntax to bring in the axios library.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing a library for HTTP requests
import axios from 'axios';
steps.expectedOutcome: The axios library is imported and ready to use for API calls.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing axios correctly from 'axios'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the import syntax. You need to import axios from 'axios'.

steps.title: Create main application structure and entry point
steps.instruction: Create a function named App that will serve as the main entry point for your ecommerce application. The function should return a div element with the id 'app'.
steps.hint: Define a function named App that returns a div element. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.seedCode:
// Import axios here

// Create your App function here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an App function that returns a div element, establishing the main container for your ecommerce application.
successCriteria: An App function is defined that returns a div element with id 'app'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your App function returns a div element. Check your function syntax and return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App function isn't properly defined. Remember to create a function named App that returns a div element.

steps.title: Initialize product data state
steps.instruction: Inside your App function, initialize a state variable named 'products' with an empty array as its initial value.
steps.hint: You'll need to use the useState hook to create state. The initial value should be an empty array [].
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state with an empty array
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App function will have a 'products' state variable initialized to an empty array, ready to store product data.
successCriteria: The 'products' state variable is declared using useState with an empty array as initial value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState to create a state variable named 'products' with an initial value of an empty array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: create a state variable called 'products' inside the App function using useState, starting with an empty array.

steps.title: Create function to fetch product data
steps.instruction: Inside your App function, create a function named fetchProducts that will handle fetching product data from an API.
steps.hint: Define a function using either function declaration or arrow function syntax. The function can be empty or return a promise for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: A fetchProducts function is defined inside the App component, ready to contain data fetching logic.
successCriteria: The fetchProducts function is created inside the App function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the fetchProducts function is defined inside the App function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchProducts function should be created inside the App function. Try adding it between the state initialization and the return statement.

steps.title: Create function to add items to cart
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a function named addToCart that takes a product object as a parameter.
steps.hint: The function should be defined inside the component so it can access the cart state. Use a function declaration or arrow function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The addToCart function is defined and ready to implement cart logic in later steps.
successCriteria: The addToCart function is created inside the App component with a product parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function is named exactly 'addToCart' and takes a product parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The addToCart function isn't properly defined. Check that it's inside the App component and has the correct name and parameter.

steps.title: Build product listing markup
steps.instruction: Inside your App component's return statement, add a <div> element with a class of 'product-list' after the existing <h1> element. This will serve as the container for your product listings.
steps.hint:
You can add a new
element with the class attribute set to 'product-list' right after the closing tag.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your App component will now have a dedicated container element ready to hold product listings.
successCriteria: A <div> element with className="product-list" is added after the <h1> element in the return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added a <div> element with the correct class name after the <h1>.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to add a container element specifically for our product listings.

steps.title: Display product data in listings
steps.instruction: Inside your product-list container, map through the products state array to render each product's name, price, and an 'Add to Cart' button.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the products array to generate product cards. Each card should display the product name, price, and a button that calls addToCart with the product.
steps.expectedOutcome: The product listing area will show dynamic product cards with name, price, and interactive 'Add to Cart' buttons.
successCriteria: The product-list container renders product cards using map, each displaying product name, price, and a button wired to addToCart.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure each product card includes the product name, price, and a button that calls addToCart with the product.
steps.feedbackWrong: The product data isn't being displayed correctly. Check that you're mapping through the products array and rendering the required elements for each product.

steps.title: Wire event handlers to product and cart buttons
steps.instruction: Add onClick handlers to the 'Add to Cart' buttons in your product listings and the 'Remove' buttons in your shopping cart, connecting them to the appropriate handler functions.
steps.hint: Look for the button elements you created earlier in the product and cart markup. Add onClick attributes that call your addToCart and removeFromCart functions with the correct product or item ID.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: wiring a button click to a handler
<button onClick={() => handleAction(item.id)}>Action</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'Add to Cart' and 'Remove' buttons will be interactive, triggering the appropriate cart management functions when clicked.
successCriteria: Both product 'Add to Cart' buttons and cart 'Remove' buttons have onClick handlers that call the correct handler functions with appropriate arguments.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some event handlers, but check if all required buttons have onClick attributes and are calling the correct functions with proper arguments.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons don't have the required onClick handlers yet. Make sure to add onClick attributes to both 'Add to Cart' and 'Remove' buttons that call your handler functions.
